papers.title: Natural-language cohort queries on a hospital data platform: accuracy and provenance in a real-world evaluation
papers.abstract: Background: Accessing routinely collected clinical data for research remains technically demanding across heterogeneous hospital systems. This proof-of-concept study aimed to evaluate the accuracy and query-level traceability of a commercial natural-language (NL) data-query platform implemented at a university hospital. Methods: An on-premises data integration platform with an NL query interface (AIRE; Briya, Tel Aviv, Israel) was connected to the institutional health data platform across three tertiary-care hospitals under an approved pseudonymization and governance framework. Implementation comprised regulatory and governance approval, and IT deployment. Twenty-five NL prompts addressing cohort identification and characterization in an adult ICD-10 C71-coded brain-tumor cohort (n = 1,594) were evaluated against manually written reference SQL and checked for a corresponding executed query in the exported log. Responses were classified into five categories. Prompts with unanswered or incorrect responses were re-posed in a new thread. Results: The platform was implemented over two years. Fifteen of 25 responses were exact (n = 11), concordant after definition alignment (n = 1), or incorrect but traceable from the logged SQL (n = 3); six were plausible but incorrect without a logged query, and four remained unanswered. No incorrect unlogged result recurred in a new thread. Across the initial and repeat evaluations, 22 of 23 logged responses were correct or traceable, whereas all eight unlogged responses were incorrect. Conclusions: Implementation was feasible but required substantial local institutional preparation. The NL interface reproduced SQL-derived results when definitions were explicit, while query-level provenance and verification of the displayed result were critical for identifying unreliable outputs.

papers.title: Exploring Data Augmentation for Stroke Severity Prediction: How Generative AI Enhances EEG Signal Classification
papers.abstract: In clinical datasets, data augmentation is often avoided because it can remove important unusual values, known as outliers, which are important for understanding diseases accurately. However, clinical EEG datasets often suffer from two key limitations: small sample sizes and class imbalance, which significantly reduce classification performance. To overcome these challenges, this study applies generative AI-based data augmentation techniques with a carefully designed hybrid pipeline that effectively enhances performance even on limited EEG data. Using EEG signals from 50 brain stroke patients, we investigate both traditional oversampling methods (SMOTE and ADASYN) and advanced generative models, including WGAN and WGAN-GP. Our proposed pipeline involves preprocessing EEG recordings, extracting comprehensive statistical and frequency-domain features, applying feature reduction, and evaluating multiple machine learning classifiers. Experimental results show that the combination of SelectKBest feature selection, SVM classifier, and WGAN-GP augmentation achieves the highest classification accuracy of 72%, outperforming other methods. This work introduces a novel hybrid approach for EEG-based stroke severity classification, demonstrating that generative augmentation, when integrated properly, can significantly improve performance on small clinical datasets. To the best of our knowledge, this combination of techniques has not been explored before on any dataset, providing a solid foundation for future research in automated EEG-based stroke diagnosis.

papers.title: User-Informed Design of a Psychological Support Social Pet Robot for Community-Dwelling People With Long-Term Physical Disabilities: A Formative Study
papers.abstract: Background. Community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities may experience pain that interferes with daily and social activities and is associated with poorer mental wellbeing. A home-based psychological support social pet robot could offer mood check-ins, companionship, supportive interaction, and mindfulness guidance for community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities. Preliminary evidence is needed to understand their preferences and translate them into candidate design requirements. Objective. This study aimed to identify preliminary needs and preferences to inform a psychological support social pet robot for community-dwelling people with long-term physical disabilities, offering mood check-ins, companionship, and mindfulness guidance at home. Methods. We conducted a 3-phase formative user-informed design study comprising initial concept development, qualitative target user interviews, and a design workshop. Six community-dwelling adults with long-term physical disabilities took part in the interviews, and one participant also answered the workshop questions by telephone. Four authors used modified workshop materials to synthesize the interview findings and separate responses into an early product plan. Results. Qualitative content analysis of the interview transcripts produced 5 themes. These were emotional support, soft touch and appearance, mindfulness delivery, context of use, and ease of use and accessibility. Participants expressed preferences about companionship, touch, use settings, and interaction effort. The author workshop combined these findings with author and technical judgments to develop candidate requirements for dialogue and mindfulness delivery. The resulting psychological support concept combined mood check-ins and companion-oriented interaction with flexible mindfulness guidance. The design also needed to consider pain and daily routines. After the workshop, the authors developed a physical proof-of-concept prototype. It implemented only part of the candidate requirements and included additional author or technical choices. Conclusions. For this small community-dwelling sample, target user input showed that home use, physical access, companionship, and flexible support were important. Mindfulness was one component of the broader psychological support role, alongside mood check-ins and optional companion interaction. The prototype illustrates but does not validate the early requirements. Further studies should include people with a wider range of long-term physical disabilities and test usability, accessibility, privacy, and nursing value. Keywords. social pet robots; user-informed design; psychological support; mindfulness; long-term physical disabilities; community dwelling; user centered design; human robot interaction; mental health; qualitative research

papers.title: Room-Aware Transformer for Activities of Daily Living Recognition in Adults with Mild Neurocognitive Disorder Using Ambient Sensors: Development and Evaluation Study
papers.abstract: ABSTRACT Background: Unobtrusive recognition of activities of daily living (ADLs) from ambient sensors may support longitudinal assessment of everyday functioning in adults with mild neurocognitive disorder (mild NCD). However, real-world activity recognition is complicated by heterogeneous home layouts, sensor configurations, routines, and class distributions. Objective: This study evaluated whether a room-aware Transformer that preserves location-specific sensor structure improves participant-level ADL recognition relative to a global Transformer and a stacked unidirectional long short-term memory (LSTM) network. Methods: Following pilot feasibility testing with two adult volunteers, we analyzed five homes of adults with mild NCD, comprising 92,765 minute-level observations across 67 annotated home-days. Motion, temperature, illuminance, humidity, and door-contact data were aligned to participant activity logs. The original labels were harmonized into eight categories. Models were developed separately for each home using 10-, 30-, and 60-minute windows. Complete calendar days were assigned to mutually exclusive training, validation, and chronological test sets, and no sequence crossed a day or partition boundary. The same partitions and evaluation procedures were used for all three architectures. Performance was assessed on held-out test days using accuracy, per-class F1 score, and micro- and macro-averaged one-versus-rest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Results: The room-aware Transformer achieved the highest or tied accuracy in 9 of 15 home-window comparisons. Its accuracy ranged from 0.27 to 0.57, micro-AUC from 0.57 to 0.82, and macro-AUC from 0.54 to 0.78. Across the 15 settings, mean accuracy was similar for the room-aware and global Transformers and higher than for the LSTM. Mean micro-AUC and macro-AUC were marginally higher for the global Transformer than for the room-aware Transformer. The room-aware model showed its clearest gains in selected contexts, including Homes C and E at 10 minutes and Home A at 60 minutes, but no architecture or temporal window was uniformly optimal. Sleep/Rest was the most consistently recognized activity, whereas low-support activities frequently had low F1 scores despite moderate or high AUC values. Conclusions: Room-specific feature processing provided context-dependent gains in participant-level ADL classification, particularly for accuracy in several home-window settings. The marked variation across homes, activities, and temporal windows supports personalized model development, class-sensitive evaluation, and validation in larger and more diverse residential samples before clinical use. Keywords: activities of daily living; mild neurocognitive disorder; ambient sensors; deep learning; artificial intelligence

papers.title: Randomized Trial Protocol: Head-to-Head Comparison of Two Ambient Artificial Intelligence Documentation Tools on Clinician Usability
papers.abstract: Abstract Background: Ambient AI documentation reduces documentation burden and electronic health record (EHR) time for ambulatory clinicians. Newer features also queue orders and offer some level of coding support for clinician review. This study compares two commercial products deployed at UCLA Health. Objective: To compare Nabla and Epic Systems, Inc. ambient AI solution among ambulatory clinicians at UCLA Health on usability, documentation burden, perceived note quality, adoption, EHR time and productivity, clinician-reported experience with order queueing and coding support, coding and billing patterns and integrity, work productivity, and patient-reported communication experience. Methods: Two-arm parallel-group randomized trial, 1:1, among 374 ambulatory clinicians at a single academic health system who hold an active license for a standalone ambient application (Nabla). Randomization is covariate-constrained where cohort size permits, balancing age, sex, half-day clinic sessions, specialty group, and baseline System Usability Scale (SUS) score. Intervention runs 11/9/2026 to 1/17/2027, with the first four weeks as lead-in. The primary outcome is SUS score at follow-up, compared between arms. Analysis is by intention-to-treat using mixed-effects models. Ethics and dissemination: Determined exempt by the UCLA Institutional Review Board (IRB-26-2147). Survey completion indicates consent. No patient-level data are collected. Findings will directly inform operational decision making and will be published regardless of direction.

papers.title: Automated MRI-Based Segmentation of the Cranio-Cervical Venous System Using a Dedicated Deep Learning Pipeline
papers.abstract: PURPOSE To develop an automated magnetic resonance imaging based segmentation pipeline for the cranio-cervical venous system (CCVS), a complex anatomical network for which no dedicated segmentation tool is currently available. MATERIALS AND METHODS A retrospective single-center cohort of 194 contrast-enhanced cranio-cervical MRI examinations acquired between 2019 and 2024 was used. Manual reference segmentations were performed on 50 examinations using 3D Slicer. A nnU-Net v2-based segmentation model was trained through an iterative process combining automatic segmentation, manual correction, and retraining. Segmentation performance was assessed using the Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC). The complete processing pipeline was integrated into an open-source software application, VenousNetworkAnalyzer (VNA). RESULTS The final model achieved a mean DSC of 0.94 (95% CI, 0.93-0.95) in five-fold cross-validation on 106 examinations with manual reference segmentations. Iterative optimization progressively reduced manual processing time from approximately 10 hours of fully manual segmentation to less than 10 minutes of manual correction per patient. Application of the final model to the entire cohort enabled the generation of patient-specific three-dimensional reconstructions of the cranio-cervical venous system. The segmentation workflow was successfully integrated into the VNA software environment, allowing automated processing and visualization of MRI datasets. CONCLUSION This study demonstrates the feasibility of automated segmentation of the cranio-cervical venous system from contrast-enhanced MRI using a dedicated deep-learning pipeline. The resulting reduction in processing time and integration into an open-source software platform provide a foundation for future large-scale anatomical studies of cranio-cervical venous draina

papers.title: OPEN: A Community-Informed Metadata Framework for Interoperable Computable Phenotypes
papers.abstract: Objective: To identify community - prioritized metadata for reporting and sharing computable phenotypes (CPs), develop a cross-library candidate framework, assess alignment between user requirements and library metadata, and test the feasibility of metadata exchange. Materials and Methods: We combined an international, library - led effort by the Open PhEnomics Network (OPEN) consortium with a UK community consensus-building exercise aimed at improving the FAIRness (Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, Reusable) of CPs. The consortium performed a cross-library field comparison and literature review to inform candidate fields, refined through consortium consensus. The community approach was developed through stakeholder interviews, a survey, and workshop, guided by a working group. Community requirements were interpretively mapped to the resulting framework and classified into conformance tiers. Interoperability was tested by manually and programmatically mapping diabetes-related phenotypes across libraries. Results: The library - led process produced 23 candidate fields spanning phenotype description, data/technical details, and performance domains. Thirteen fields aligned across all five libraries, and 22 fields aligned with published CP library desiderata. Interoperability testing successfully catalogued phenotypes through manual mapping, with API - mediated mapping achieving 63 - 76% metadata field completeness across libraries. A community survey (n=124 respondents) identified six metadata elements with majority support as mandatory: description, coding terminology, phenotype type, version history, unique identifier, and data source. Logic representation and validation requirements were rated as mostly context-dependent. Community - identified priorities showed strong alignment with the OPEN framework, though some requirements were only partially represented. Discussion: Through a consensus - based, community - driven approach, we established a CP framework enabling interoperability across libraries. Conclusion: OPEN provides a credible, community - informed foundation for a FAIR CP metadata standard.

papers.title: Multi-Agent Generative Artificial Intelligence for Transfusion Reaction Feature Extraction
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Many transfusion reactions are not reported to hemovigilance systems, and the features needed to recognize them are often documented only in free-text clinical notes. We sought to develop and evaluate an open-source, multi-agent artificial intelligence (AI) pipeline to extract transfusion reaction features defined by the National Healthcare Safety Network (NHSN) Hemovigilance Module from clinical notes. METHODS: We curated 181 features from the NHSN protocol and developed a multi-stage pipeline that extracted features, their timing, and clinical details from free-text notes. Three open-weight large language models (Qwen 3.6-27B, GPT-OSS-120B, and Kimi K3) were applied to 50 notes from expert-written scenarios, published case reports, and MIMIC-IV discharge summaries. Two physicians independently evaluated every model output in a blinded interface. The primary analysis was restricted to feature occurrences with concordant physician assessments. RESULTS: Physicians agreed on 1,201 of 1,343 co-rated feature occurrences (89.4%; Krippendorff's alpha 0.73). Precision was above 0.98 for all models. Sensitivity was 0.774 (95% CI 0.745-0.800) for Kimi K3, 0.636 (0.604-0.667) for GPT-OSS-120B, and 0.624 (0.593-0.655) for Qwen 3.6-27B, and specificity ranged from 0.952 to 0.991. Omissions accounted for more than 94% of false negatives. Timing and clinical details were judged supported or reasonable in more than 92% and 97% of assessments, respectively. Results were consistent across note sources and in analyses including discordant assessments. CONCLUSION: Multi-agent AI pipelines provide a feasible method for extracting transfusion reaction signals from clinical notes with high precision. Our work may have applications in active hemovigilance, reaction classification, and big data research.

papers.title: BioLT: Streaming Biosignal Modeling
papers.abstract: Clinical biosignals such as ECG, PPG, and EEG are increasingly acquired as hours-long streams from bedside monitors and wearables, yet existing analysis pipelines almost universally operate on isolated short windows of around 10 seconds and cannot process the long, irregular, frequently interrupted signals. We introduce BioLT, a streaming decoder-only framework for long-context biosignal modeling that turns any window-level feature extractor or pretrained biosignal foundation model into a streaming model. BioLT combines (i) a discontinuity-aware encoding that exposes the inter-window elapsed time as an explicit input channel, so that the decoder can learn to model these gaps as clinically meaningful information, and (ii) a fixed-size compressed memory bank supervised with cumulative summary statistics, which keeps both training and inference linear in the recording length while preserving long-range context. We evaluate on CPSC-2021, VitalDB, MC-MED, and CHB-MIT for arrhythmia, sepsis, and seizure detection and for forecasting up to 20 minutes ahead, using domain features and embeddings from six biosignal foundation models. Across 21 dataset-feature settings, BioLT achieves the highest detection AUROC in 15 and the highest 20-minute forecasting AUROC in 13 settings, and shows consistent performance gains over state-of-the-art snapshot foundation-model embeddings. These highlight the importance of modeling how streaming biosignal representations evolve over time, beyond improving window-level representations alone.

papers.title: Accelerometer Data Harmonization and Feature Engineering for Gait Analytics
papers.abstract: Gait analytics is utilized for a wide range of health-related applications, ranging from fitness tracking to medical diagnostics, and beyond. Inertial measurement units that are ubiquitously available in mobile devices provide an accessible means of gait analysis but differences in sensor specifications, placement, and recording protocols limit comparability across studies. This study developed and evaluated an analysis-centered data warehouse and standardized quality-assessed processing pipeline to facilitate the integration and joint analysis of heterogeneous gait accelerometer data. Six publicly available datasets including a total of 935 persons were integrated into a star-schema data warehouse, and feature comparability was assessed across datasets and sensor locations. Gender classification served as a proof-of-concept downstream analysis. Gait-cycle extraction, which serves as foundation for feature extraction, was successfully achieved with an accuracy above 99% for the dataset that provides ground truth information. Comparability varied across datasets and sensor configurations, with correlation coefficients between average gait cycles ranging from 0.5 to close to 1.0. Centrally positioned sensors generally show greater correspondence than peripheral sensors, although differences in statistical features persist even between sensors at nominally identical locations. Gender classification performance remains largely near chance level, and no consistent benefit from pooling datasets could be established. These findings demonstrate that heterogeneous gait accelerometer data can be integrated and processed within a common analytical framework, but standardized processing alone does not ensure comparability of the resulting features. The proposed open-source framework implemented in Python provides a foundation for reproducible cross-study gait analysis and for investigating residual heterogeneity associated with datasets and sensor configurations.

papers.title: Methodological Adherence, Reporting Completeness, and Risk of Bias in AI-Assisted Systematic Reviews: A Matched Meta-Research Study
papers.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to accelerate systematic reviews that inform clinical practice and policy. However, evidence on the methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias of completed AI-assisted reviews is limited. Objective: To compare methodological adherence, reporting completeness, and risk of bias between published systematic reviews with reported AI assistance and matched reviews with no reported AI use, and to assess AI-use transparency. Methods: We conducted a matched-cohort meta-research study of English-language, peer-reviewed health systematic reviews. AI-assisted reviews published during 2023--2025 were matched 1:2 to reviews with no reported AI use using individualized MEDLINE searches targeting publication timing, clinical domain, review type, and meta-analysis status. When more than two eligible comparators were available, two were randomly selected. AI assistance was defined as reported use during searching, screening, data extraction, risk-of-bias assessment, evidence synthesis, or substantive drafting. Full texts and supplementary materials were examined to classify reported AI use. The primary outcome was a prespecified modified 13-item AMSTAR-2 methodological-adherence score (range 0 -- 13; noninferiority margin &-1 point). Secondary outcomes included PRISMA 2020 reporting completeness and ROBIS risk of bias; AI-use transparency was assessed descriptively. Adapted 13-item AMSTAR-2 confidence categories were summarized descriptively, while critical- and noncritical-domain adherence was examined in exploratory adjusted analyses. Multivariable regression models adjusted for journal impact tier, funding reporting, formal review-group affiliation, review-team size, and review-question type, using cluster-robust standard errors by matched set. Sensitivity analyses included matched-set fixed-effects models. The study was registered on the Open Science Framework (DOI: 10.17605/OSF.IO/Q5JRW). Results: The cohort included 231 systematic reviews: 77 AI-assisted and 154 with no reported AI use. Mean 13-item AMSTAR-2 scores were 7.58 and 9.63, respectively. In multivariable-adjusted analyses, AI-assisted reviews scored 1.64 points lower (95% CI &-2.37 to &- 0.91); noninferiority was not demonstrated. PRISMA adherence was estimated to be 4.7 percentage points lower among AI-assisted reviews in primary adjusted analyses (95% CI &-8.9 to &-0.6) and 6.4 points lower in matched-set fixed-effects analyses (95% CI &-10.7 to &-2.1). Among reviews with assessable ROBIS ratings, 75.0% of AI-assisted reviews and 65.6% of comparators were rated low risk (adjusted difference +17.8 percentage points; 95% CI 2.7 to 33.0). Among AI-assisted reviews, model version or date was reported in 42.9%, prompts or parameters in 55.8%, and data-governance or ethics considerations in 9.1%. Conclusions: Reviews reporting AI assistance had lower methodological-adherence scores and had less complete reporting, despite more favorable risk-of-bias ratings. These findings provide an early warning that AI-assisted systematic reviews may require stronger safeguards, human verification, and transparency to support trust.

papers.title: Agentic Pipeline for Large-Scale Clinical Data Queries in Enterprise Electronic Health Records
papers.abstract: Using electronic health record (EHR) data to answer clinical research questions is challenging. It requires understanding the research question, finding relevant information across different sources, and combining that information to produce meaningful results. We developed an agentic large language model (LLM) pipeline that decomposes investigator-authored requests into source-specific tasks, generates and executes SQL on EHR, integrates structured and unstructured EHR evidence, and applies study-specific clinical note adjudication. We evaluated this workflow against data analyst-identified cohorts across 50 pediatric orthopedic clinical data query requests. Of these, 43 were included in manual-review-adjusted performance analyses. The median adjusted positive predictive value, sensitivity among patients identified by either approach, and corresponding F1 score were 0.93 (95% CI, 0.88-0.98), 0.92 (95% CI, 0.90-0.95) and 0.90 (95% CI, 0.87-0.94), respectively. These findings support the feasibility of translating natural-language research intent into executable, autonomous multi-stage EHR workflows.

papers.title: A Cross-Dataset Audit of Discrimination and Conformal Prediction Coverage in Keystroke-Based Parkinson's Disease Classi cation
papers.abstract: Typing dynamics are being investigated as a digital behavioral marker for Parkinson's disease (PD), but the cross-dataset reliability of typing-based classi ers remains uncertain. We evaluated four public datasets (475 par ticipants; 270 with PD and 205 controls) across 12 transfer directions using split conformal prediction targeting 90% marginal coverage. In all three pri mary directions, coverage was below the 0.90 target and the one-sided tests remained signi cant after Holm correction: 0.598 (95% CI, 0.4830.704) for Tappy[->]MIT, 0.850 (0.7880.899) for MIT[->]Tappy, and 0.732 (0.6840.777) for clinical[->]self-reported transfer. Discrimination and coverage did not con sistently change together: LightGBM had lower AUC than logistic regression in all 12 directions but higher coverage in 11, with larger prediction sets. Class-conditional coverage varied by target cohort: PD-conditional cover age was 0.214 for Tappy[->]MIT, whereas healthy-control coverage was 0.700 for MIT[->]Tappy and 0.627 for clinical[->]self-reported transfer. Recalibration with 9 and 18 labeled target participants raised the lower condence bound above 0.80 in the latter two directions; in Tappy[->]MIT, it remained below 0.80 even with 25 labels. Weighted conformal prediction yielded coverage of 0.9181.000 without target labels but returned the full label set for 86% 100% of participants. Stress tests did not reproduce the observed coverage patterns, and black-box shift estimation did not support pure label shift as the dominant explanation for Tappy[->]MIT. Evaluating typing dynamics as a digital marker for PD requires cross-dataset assessment of discrimination, marginal and class-conditional coverage, and recovery costs. Clinical screen ing utility has not been established.

papers.title: An explainable, bias-audited machine learning model to detect hidden hepatitis C from region-wide real-world health records
papers.abstract: BackgroundAlthough direct-acting antivirals have transformed hepatitis C virus (HCV) treatment, 25-30% of active infections in Spain remain undiagnosed. We aimed to develop and validate an interpretable machine-learning model to identify undiagnosed HCV infection using only data already recorded within the health system. Materials and MethodsWe conducted a retrospective, population-based cohort study using the Andalusian Population Health Database (BPS). Individuals diagnosed with HCV between 2017 and 2024 (n=25,028) were matched, up to 10:1, to controls by birth year, sex, and health district. An Explainable Boosting Machine was trained on 2017-2022 data, with a threshold set in a 2023 validation set to guarantee [≥]60% sensitivity, then evaluated unmodified in an independent, non-matched, population-representative 2024 sample approximating real-world screening. Predictors comprised chronic-disease diagnoses and laboratory summary statistics recorded [≥]30 days before the index date; age and sex were excluded as matching variables. Predictors reflecting socioeconomic proxies or matching artefacts (pharmaceutical co-payment category, a zone-level deprivation index) were removed after explainability review. ResultsIn the independent test set, the model achieved an AUC of 0.837 (0.826 in validation), sensitivity 63.5%, specificity 91.8%, positive predictive value 7.0%, and negative predictive value 99.6%. Leading predictors were minimum alanine aminotransferase, HIV infection, dependence on non-tobacco substances, and platelet-count statistics, forming a clinically coherent, laboratory- and comorbidity-driven profile. ConclusionAn explainable model built exclusively from routine electronic health record data can identify undiagnosed HCV infection with discrimination comparable to previously published tools, evaluated under conditions approximating true population prevalence. Bias-auditing was feasible without sacrificing interpretability, supporting a scalable, equity-conscious instrument for the final phase of HCV elimination.

papers.title: Figure format and the accuracy of AI-assisted reconstruction of Kaplan-Meier survival data
papers.abstract: Reconstructing participant-level data from published Kaplan-Meier curves supports meta-analysis and other secondary survival analyses when original trial records are unavailable. Researchers may use original PDF figures or screenshots, which can look alike but retain different information. We assessed how converting vector figures to images affects reconstruction by a language model that can inspect files and execute code. We generated 64 independent two-arm datasets across four scenarios combining 100 or 1,000 participants per arm with proportional or crossing hazards. Each figure was supplied as a native vector PDF and a matched 300-dpi PNG to Opus 5.5 through Claude Code under the same instructions. Outcomes compared reconstructed records with the original observed records: time-averaged absolute curve error through 24 months, error in the between-group restricted mean survival time difference, and error in the Cox log-hazard ratio. Native PDFs had lower curve error in all 64 completed pairs, including replacements for incomplete runs. Mean errors were 0.000029 and 0.1047 percentage points for PDF and PNG, respectively; the paired difference was -0.1047 (95% confidence interval, -0.1194 to -0.0909). PNG errors in the restricted mean survival time difference and log-hazard ratio were small: mean absolute errors were 0.0084 months and 0.0027. Lower resolution and compression increased curve errors; embedding unchanged pixels in a PDF did not restore vector accuracy. Some PNG runs exceeded the instructed revision limit, so results describe the implemented workflow rather than performance under a strictly enforced limit. Preserving vector information improved reconstruction fidelity in this workflow, but the observed differences do not establish clinically consequential changes in treatment estimates. Validation against reported survival summaries and event counts remains necessary. Generalization to published clinical figures and other model workflows requires further evaluation. Author summaryClinical studies often publish survival graphs without sharing the underlying patient records. Researchers can estimate event and follow-up times from these graphs and use them to combine evidence across studies. Artificial intelligence may reduce the work involved, but its accuracy can depend on how a figure is supplied. We studied whether an original vector PDF and a matching image led the same artificial intelligence system to reconstruct different data. Using simulated studies allowed us to compare every reconstruction with known records. The system could write and run computer code. It recovered curves more accurately from vector PDFs, which preserved readable curve coordinates, than from images containing only pixels. However, average differences in treatment estimates were small. Lower-resolution and compressed images produced larger errors, and putting an image inside a PDF did not recover the lost information. Our findings support preserving original vector figures when possible. Even when reconstructed KM curves closely matched the originals, the reconstructed data sometimes contained incorrect event counts. The results apply to one computational workflow using clean simulated figures; performance with published clinical figures, other systems, and consistently enforced revision limits still needs evaluation. Data availability statementAll data used in this study were simulated. The project repository is https://github.com/ FionaShiyinLi/km-curve-reconstruction-study. The reproducibility materials comprise reference records, input figures, reconstructed records, dataset-level results, reconstruction instructions, random seeds, and generation, reconstruction, and analysis code.

papers.title: Deep learning screening of otoscopic images for ENT referral: development, validation and deployment of NHREF OtoScan
papers.abstract: BackgroundMiddle and external ear disease is common and largely treatable, but accurate otoscopic interpretation requires training that is scarce outside specialist ENT services. Published deep learning models for otoscopy report high accuracy, yet most are optimised for closed-set classification rather than the referral decision a non-specialist actually makes, report uncalibrated probabilities, and do not report the near-duplicate controls that video-derived otoscopic datasets demand. We developed, validated and deployed a screening aid framed around referral rather than diagnosis. MethodsWe merged 4,763 otoscopic images from 16 folders across three public datasets into 12 clinically meaningful classes. Every image was passed through a single field-of-view normalisation function (crop to the illuminated field, square, resize to 224 px, mask to one fixed circle) shared identically by training and inference, to remove the framing cue that otherwise identifies the source dataset. Because one source is video-derived, images were grouped by cosine similarity of generic ImageNet features (threshold 0.93, joined transitively) and whole groups assigned to a single split, giving 3,326 training, 719 validation and 718 test images. A MobileNetV2 backbone initialised from ImageNet was fine-tuned from block_9_expand. Probabilities were averaged over the eight dihedral transforms of each image and temperature-scaled. The referral score was one minus the probability of a normal ear, and its threshold was set on the validation abnormal ears as the highest value still meeting a target sensitivity of 97%, applied with an inclusive comparison. Model selection, calibration and threshold were frozen before the test split was scored once. ResultsOn the 718 held-out test images, referral sensitivity was 97.0% (95% CI 95.1-98.2) and specificity 75.6% (95% CI 69.4-80.8), with AUROC 0.974 for abnormal versus normal; a cluster bootstrap over the 363 similarity groups in the test split widens those intervals to 93.8-99.6% and 66.0-83.4% respectively. Of 501 abnormal ears, 15 were not referred; 11 of these were myringosclerosis and none was cholesteatoma. Twelve-class macro F1 was 0.686, balanced accuracy 68.3%, and accuracy 85.0% (86.2% with chronic subtypes merged). Temperature scaling (T = 1.2) reduced expected calibration error from 0.0498 to 0.0430. A low-confidence flag fired on 4.0% of test images, separating 87.2% accuracy on unflagged from 31.0% on flagged cases. Recall was consistently highest on the largest source dataset and fell on the other two, for example acute otitis media 95.5% on source A versus 50.0% on source B. ConclusionsA compact, calibrated model run on ordinary CPU hardware achieved the pre-specified 97% referral sensitivity with clinically interpretable failure modes. The source-stratified gap, and an earlier perceptual-hash split that inflated scores until it was corrected, indicate that headline accuracy in this field is strongly dependent on leakage control and acquisition style. The system is deployed with mandatory specialist review, a daily backtest and approval-gated retraining, so that prospective performance on local equipment is measured rather than assumed. It is research software and not a medical device. RegistrationNot applicable. This was retrospective model development on public data. FundingFunded by the Nawaloka Hospitals Research and Education Foundation.

papers.title: Application of Machine Learning and Deep Learning in diagnosis Covid19
papers.abstract: Predicting the progression of COVID-19 in hospitalised patients was an important challenge during the pandemic, particularly when healthcare resources were limited. This study investigates the use of machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) models to predict three clinical outcomes: death, admission to the intensive care unit (ICU), and clinical status (improvement or worsening). The study uses two patient datasets: an Algerian cohort of 80 patients from the Internal Medicine Department of the University Hospital Centre of Constantine, collected between July and August 2020, and a French cohort of 99 patients collected between March and May 2020. Five ML classifiers were evaluated: logistic regression (LR), k-nearest neighbours (KNN), classification and regression trees (CART), Naive Bayes (NB), and support vector machines (SVM). Their performance was examined in combination with three feature-selection methods: analysis of variance (ANOVA), mutual information (MI), and recursive feature elimination (RFE). The results were also compared with multilayer perceptron (MLP) models using one to five hidden layers. Model evaluation included 30 repetitions of five-fold cross-validation on the training data, followed by evaluation on a separate hold-out test set. The results showed that selecting 20 features generally provided better cross-validated accuracy than selecting 30 features or using the full feature set. The best-performing classifier-feature-selection combination varied across the six dataset-outcome tasks. LR combined with RFE was selected for three tasks, LR combined with ANOVA for one task, and CART combined with ANOVA for two tasks. The selected ML models achieved test-set accuracies ranging from 0.47 to 0.95 and higher accuracy than the average MLP results in five of the six tasks. These findings suggest that ML methods can be useful for exploring clinical outcomes in hospitalised COVID-19 patients. However, the small sample sizes and limitations of the available data mean that the results should be interpreted with caution. Further evaluation using larger and independent patient datasets is needed before these models can be considered for clinical use.

papers.title: First-trimester nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling during home sleep testing and later pregnancy complications: a secondary analysis of the nuMoM2b cohort
authors: M. B. van der Hout-van der Jagt
papers.abstract: We tested whether direction-specific nocturnal cardiorespiratory coupling (CRC) in the first trimester differed in pregnancies that later developed obstetric complications. The analysis included 2,504 nulliparous women from the nuMoM2b cohort with valid level 3 home sleep recordings at 6-13 weeks gestation. Bidirectional CRC between RR intervals and abdominal respiratory effort was quantified using bivariate phase-rectified signal averaging in consecutive 5-min segments. Coupling strength, local transition dynamics, and waveform irregularity were summarized by nightly mean and standard deviation. Associations with gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM; n = 111), preeclampsia (n = 149), preterm birth (n = 192), and fetal macrosomia (n = 186) were examined using proportional-odds models with CRC feature quintile as the ordered outcome. Models included all four complications simultaneously and adjusted for maternal age, pre-pregnancy body mass index, race and ethnicity, gestational age at recording, relevant medical and family history, medication use, and apnea-hypopnea index >5 events{middle dot}h-1. Holm correction was applied across outcomes. GDM was associated with lower respiration-to-heart rate coupling strength (cumulative odds ratio, 0.45; 95% CI, 0.31-0.64; P < 0.001) and shallower slope at the anchor point (0.63; 0.45-0.89; P = 0.03). Fetal macrosomia was associated with lower within-night variability in heart rate-to-respiration waveform irregularity (0.59; 0.45-0.77; P < 0.001). No associations with preeclampsia or preterm birth remained significant after correction. Direction-specific differences in nocturnal CRC were detectable in the first trimester in pregnancies that later developed GDM or resulted in fetal macrosomia. New & NoteworthyUsing home sleep recordings from 2,504 women in the first trimester, we found direction-specific differences in maternal cardiorespiratory coupling in pregnancies that later developed gestational diabetes or resulted in fetal macrosomia. Gestational diabetes was associated with lower respiration-to-heart rate coupling strength, whereas fetal macrosomia was associated with lower within-night variability in heart rate-to-respiration coupling irregularity. No significant associations were observed for preeclampsia or preterm birth.

papers.title: Evaluating uncertainty for detecting performance loss and guiding deferral after model transfer between hospital systems
papers.abstract: Clinical prediction models often perform worse after transfer between hospital systems, but deterioration becomes apparent only once outcomes are known. We investigated whether uncertainty measures available at prediction time warn of performance loss and can help identify individual predictions requiring review. Three neural network architectures were trained on MIMIC-IV for in-hospital mortality prediction and evaluated on eICU-CRD. Measures included predictive entropy, mutual information from Monte Carlo dropout and deep ensembles, and representation density. After transfer, AUROC fell from 0.86-0.87 to 0.76-0.77 and calibration worsened, while entropy and mutual information were lower. None of the measures reliably indicated the reduced performance. Deferring the 20% with the highest entropy reduced the remaining error rate from 17.5-20.1% to 6.3-8.0%; the deferred patients included 91-99% of false alarms but only 2-7% of missed deaths, which carried low uncertainty. Uncertainty therefore supported selective review but failed to reveal performance loss.

papers.title: Unsupervised Phenotypic Stratification of 22q11.2 Deletion Syndrome for Improved Clinical Screening
papers.abstract: Objective22q11.2 deletion syndrome (22q11DS) is the leading genetic cause of palatal anomalies, presenting a heterogeneous spectrum of clinical manifestations that complicates early diagnosis. No study has systematically investigated the co-occurrence of symptoms spanning cardiovascular, neuropsychiatric, craniofacial, immune, endocrine, renal, and familial domains within a single cohort using unsupervised learning methods for 22q11DS stratification. This study proposes a pipeline to identify subgroups and associated symptom patterns from binary clinical data, aiming to improve screening and referral for genetic testing. DesignCross-sectional, retrospective study comparing three unsupervised clustering frameworks-- K-medoids, DBSCAN, and Latent Class Analysis (LCA)--followed by association rule mining applied to individuals with confirmed deletion. SettingBrazilian Database of Craniofacial Anomalies (BBAC), a national clinical registry. ParticipantsA cohort of 297 individuals with suspected 22q11DS. Main Outcome MeasuresCluster separability (silhouette coefficient), characterization of phenotypic subgroups, and sensitivity/specificity of the current screening protocol stratified by subgroup. ResultsLCA achieved the highest cluster separability (silhouette = 0.165), yielding four distinct subgroups: Cardiac-predominant (C0), Craniofacial-palatal (C1), Neurodevelopmental-psychiatric (C2), and Mild-craniofacial (C3). Cluster coherence was confirmed by medical specialists. Quantitative protocol assessment revealed adequate overall sensitivity, with markedly lower performance for C2 and C3, identifying profiles at higher risk of being missed by current screening criteria. ConclusionsThese findings provide a data-driven basis for recalibrating symptom weights and referral thresholds, improving sensitivity for underperforming subgroups while reducing unnecessary referrals, optimizing the balance between diagnostic coverage and the financial burden of genetic testing.

papers.title: Same answer, different reasons: AI-moderated interviews uncover topics and reasoning that surveys miss.
papers.abstract: Surveys can reach large samples but capture only pre-defined answers, with identical responses often concealing very different reasoning. We tested whether AI-moderated interviews capture this reasoning at scale. In a pre-registered, randomized, counterbalanced design, 1,953 US adults from a probability-based panel and an opt-in panel completed three AI-moderated interviews as well as a section with closed-ended and open-text survey items. Topics were extracted from transcripts inductively, without a predefined codebook, and validated by a confirmatory follow-up. Participants endorsed 94% of topics as fair descriptions of what they said. 21-51% of topics from the AI interview had no counterpart in the closed-ended battery, and 17-37 percentage points net coverage over open text answers. Among respondents who gave identical closed-ended responses, their reasoning diverged widely in valence and content. AI-moderated interviews surface reasons that closed-ended and open-text items miss, and show how reasoning differs among people who answer alike.

papers.title: Preceding organ trajectories guide dynamic reassessment after apparent stabilisation in sepsis
papers.abstract: Organ scores can conceal recent instability. We studied confirmed six-hour deterioration in six organs with low recorded severity among 19,690 adults with sepsis in MIMIC-IV, eICU, CareVue and SICdb. Using a 175-variable model reduced from 552, we compared 3,072 combinations of 12 historical sources. With hourly predictions, at least four hours between alerts and 0.50 alerts per patient, the model using ten sources captured 319 eICU events versus 245 using current information alone (+30.2%; difference 74, 95% CI 49-106.5). Gains were 34.6% in CareVue (144 versus 107) and 81.5% in SICdb (49 versus 27); using six sources captured 312 eICU events. Training with incomplete records increased capture from 180 to 211 (+31) under 50% withholding. Retrieving one existing laboratory record improved timely correct organ selection from 145 to 159 (+9.7%). Repeated new low-severity measurements changed earlier history's value. Models were evaluated without retraining in 1,661 adults with pancreatitis-related conditions.

papers.title: Analytic Interoperability Framework for High-Fidelity Representation of Perioperative Electronic Health Record Data in the OMOP Common Data Model Using Clinical Representation and Analytic Concept Reconstruction
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate whether complex perioperative electronic health record (EHR) data can be represented within the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership (OMOP) Common Data Model (CDM) while preserving clinically meaningful analytic concepts. Materials and MethodsData from 31,158 consecutive adult elective surgical encounters (October 2015- September 2025) were extracted from an academic medical centers Epic Clarity database. Source concepts required for a postoperative respiratory failure dataset were manually mapped to OMOP using the OHDSI Athena vocabulary and classified by Health Level 7 equivalence categories under strict and lenient criteria. SQL-based workflows reconstructed clinical representations and analytic concepts, which were validated against the native Epic implementation. ResultsThe reference dataset comprised 28 analytic variables derived from 538 source concepts. Under strict criteria, 40.7% of mappings were equal; under lenient criteria permitting clinical equivalence despite terminology or granularity differences, 97.4% were classified as equal. OMOP achieved >99% cohort concordance. Among 31,083 shared encounters, reconstructed analytic variables showed high agreement, with meaningful differences primarily involving vasopressor infusion identification, body mass index selection, and payer assignment; admission source accounted for most discordant cohort assignments. DiscussionConcept equivalence alone incompletely characterized analytic interoperability. Reconstruction of clinical representations and analytic concepts from standardized OMOP concepts preserved analytic fidelity despite incomplete exact concept matching. ConclusionsComplex perioperative EHR data can be represented within OMOP with high implementation fidelity despite imperfect concept equivalence. Evaluating preservation of clinically meaningful analytic concepts, rather than vocabulary equivalence alone, provides a practical framework for interoperable perioperative research.

papers.title: Questioning the Benchmarks: Hidden Circularity in AQ-10 Autism Screening Datasets
papers.abstract: Autism spectrum disorder (ASD) screening increasingly relies on machine learning models trained on the AQ-10 and Q-CHAT questionnaire datasets, and these models are widely reported to reach 95 to 99 percent accuracy, so confirming whether that accuracy reflects genuine diagnostic learning is vital. This paper examines whether that accuracy reflects genuine diagnostic learning or is simply an artifact of how the datasets are built. The study compares six model families, namely Logistic Regression, Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, XGBoost, FT-Transformer, and TabNet, across three UCI AQ-10 age variants: Child (n = 290), Adolescent (n = 103), and Adult (n = 699). Most emphasis is put on separating the behavioral items that define the diagnostic label from the demographic covariates that do not, since the label itself is a threshold applied to those same items. The effectiveness of this separation is measured using a normalized Circularity Index alongside item-only and demographics-only accuracy. Evaluation of the results has shown that item-based accuracy stays at 93.2 to 100 percent even after the pre-computed result score column is removed, while demographics-only accuracy falls to 50.7 to 71.5 percent, at or below the majority-class baseline in every dataset, giving a mean Circularity Index of 0.947. The same pattern is confirmed on two independent domains outside autism screening: DASS-42 depression screening (n = 35,481, CI 0.984) and the Rosenberg Self-Esteem Scale (n = 39,076, CI 0.896). Lastly, a diagnostic heuristic named AutoCirc is introduced to flag this kind of circularity automatically using mutual information, reproducing the manual Circularity Index on three of five datasets, and a constructive eight-of-ten-item AQ-10 short form is proposed as a practical outcome of the same analysis. The results of the study confirm that high reported accuracy on these datasets reflects the scoring arithmetic of the screening instrument rather than a learned diagnostic pattern, though this does not call the AQ-10 into question as a clinical screening tool when used as intended. Further work shall seek to extend this audit to additional screening instruments, such as PHQ-9 and GAD-7, and to datasets carrying independent clinical diagnosis labels.

papers.title: Pheno+: An Electronic Health Record-Integrated, Clinician-in-the-Loop Application for Efficient Phenotyping in Clinical Genomics
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo evaluate the efficiency and diagnostic utility of Pheno+, an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated application that streamlines the generation of structured phenotypes for genomic testing and analysis. Materials and MethodsWe developed Pheno+ as a Substitutable Medical Applications and Reusable Technologies on Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (SMART on FHIR) application embedded within the University of Utah Health EHR. Pheno+ applies ClinPhen to clinician-selected clinical notes to identify candidate Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) terms, which clinicians review and curate within the EHR. We conducted an eight-case crossover evaluation comparing workflow time between Pheno+ and a standard workflow that involved physician chart review and molecular geneticist-led HPO term selection. In a separate cohort of 17 patients with confirmed monogenic diagnoses, we assessed the diagnostic utility of Pheno+-derived HPO terms by evaluating Exomiser gene prioritization performance using these terms. ResultsPheno+ reduced mean total workflow time by 66%, from 31.1 to 10.5 minutes (p < 0.001). Incorporating Pheno+-derived HPO terms improved Exomisers ability to rank the causative gene first, from 11 of 17 cases (64.7%) without phenotype input to 17 of 17 cases (100%) with phenotype input (p = 0.031). Discussion and ConclusionPheno+ reduced the time and personnel required to generate clinician-curated HPO term lists while producing phenotypes that improved causative gene prioritization. These findings support EHR-integrated, clinician-in-the-loop phenotyping as an efficient approach to generating diagnostically informative phenotype data for clinical genomic workflows.

papers.title: Identifying interstitial lung disease with large language models on clinical notes and claims
papers.abstract: BackgroundInterstitial lung disease (ILD) is a potentially fatal toxicity of immune check-point inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates. Drug-safety studies in healthcare databases identify ILD with claims-based algorithms that trade positive predictive value (PPV) against sensitivity. We assessed whether large language models (LLMs) improve on these algorithms, with and without electronic health record (EHR) notes, and whether these gains translate into measurable epidemiological benefits. MethodsIn 309 oncology patients with ILD diagnosis codes at Mass General Brigham, adjudicated by two pulmonologists, we compared 12 open-access LLMs with 20 published claims-based algorithms. LLMs received claims, EHR notes, or both, without task-specific training. Measures were PPV and yield (proportion classified positive). We projected the attenuation of a drug-induced ILD odds ratio under non-differential outcome misclassification. FindingsLLMs extended the PPV-yield frontier of the published algorithms with all three inputs. Across the 36 model-input evaluations, LLM PPV exceeded that of the best algorithm without specialist-coding requirements (Algorithm 4) by 14.3 percentage points on average. With claims alone, Qwen3-8B achieved 89.8% PPV (95% CI 78.2-95.6) at 15.9% yield, versus 86.7% at 4.9% for the highest-PPV algorithm. With notes alone, Qwen3-32B achieved 78.9% PPV at 49.2% yield, versus 64.6% at 51.1% for Algorithm 4. With combined claims and notes, Qwen3-14B achieved 100.0% PPV at 24.3% yield. Under a simulated drug-safety scenario with a true odds ratio of 3.0, the projected observed odds ratio was 2.67 with combined inputs versus 1.07 with Algorithm 4, corresponding to a 46-fold difference in the estimated sample size required for 80% power (591 versus 27,200 patients). InterpretationZero-shot LLMs offer a higher-PPV alternative to rule-based claims pheno-typing for ILD, on all three input types. Because the claims-only configuration uses the same claims data as existing algorithms, it could be deployed in administrative databases without linked notes, and may recover drug-safety signal otherwise lost to outcome misclassification. FundingNational Institute on Aging, National Library of Medicine, PCORI, and the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed up to August 2026 for studies on claims or electronic health record (EHR)-based identification of interstitial lung disease and on machine-learning or large language model (LLM) phenotyping of clinical conditions. Search terms included "interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis", "administrative claims", "computational phenotyping", "rule-based algorithms", "machine learning", and "large language models". We also screened the reference lists of relevant articles. The literature search suggested that identifying ILD in longitudinal claims data is unreliable because the relevant diagnosis codes are nonspecific, and validated rule-based algorithms face a structural tradeoff between PPV and coverage. Supervised machine-learning classifiers have outperformed rule-based ILD identification on electronic health record data, and zero-shot LLMs have already shown the ability to phenotype chronic conditions from structured codes. No study, however, had compared a zero-shot LLM head-to-head against validated, published claims-based algorithms for a specific, high-stakes drug-safety outcome on a single fixed cohort, isolated the contribution of the input substrate from that of the model, or quantified the downstream consequence for pharmacoepidemiologic effect estimation. Added value of this studyOn a single, fixed, expert-adjudicated cohort, the evaluated LLMs achieved higher positive predictive value (PPV) than all 20 published claims-based algorithms at comparable yield (the proportion of patients classified as ILD-positive), whether the models received structured claims, clinical notes, or both. Across the 36 model-input evaluations, PPV exceeded that of the most inclusive published rule by 19.7 percentage points on average, and did so in 33 of 36 evaluations. We show that clinical notes generally increased yield, while the resulting PPV-yield trade-off depended on the model and input combination. Restricting the input to a single EHR note type preserved the advantage over rule-based phenotyping in matched comparisons on the patients possessing that EHR note type. Most consequentially, this improvement reduces the sample size required to detect a hypothesised drug-ILD association from approximately 27,200 patients for the best existing algorithm for the task to 591 when using LLMs, and offer a deployable upgrade for the note-free administrative databases where rule-based algorithms are the current standard. Implications of all the available evidenceFor pharmacovigilance of treatment-related ILD, the limiting step is often not the size of the available claims database but the misclassification that erodes the very signal under surveillance. Replacing rule-based claims phenotyping algorithms with zero-shot LLM-based alternatives transforms a high-PPV, low-yield classifier into one that recovers many more patients at the same PPV, converting a classifier that can render drug-safety associations statistically invisible into one that makes them detectable in cohorts of feasible size. Pending external validation, this offers a practical route to more sensitive post-marketing surveillance of the pulmonary toxicity of immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates. More broadly, we hypothesise that this advantage is not specific to ILD: zero-shot LLM phenotyping may recover drug-safety signal for other outcomes that diagnosis codes capture poorly but that are well documented in clinical text, a possibility that warrants dedicated evaluation.

papers.title: Triage Advice From General-Purpose Language Models in Health and Everyday Situations
papers.abstract: ImportanceOne adult in 10 has consulted a chatbot for health information within 6 months, and nearly half of users do so to decide whether they need care. Referral regardless of need could add demand on stretched services. ObjectiveTo compare referral to a professional by general-purpose language models in health and non-health situations against the level of contact that human raters judged necessary. Design, Setting, and ParticipantsCross-sectional study of 4,346 responses generated in September 2026 by 53 general-purpose model configurations, released between March 2023 and September 2026 and accessed through APIs or run locally, to 82 investigator-written messages (41 health and 41 non-health). No patients were involved. ExposuresHealth vs non-health scenario. Main Outcomes and MeasuresProfessional referral, unconditional or conditional on a future change or on doubt, coded by 3 language models and compared with the level of contact that physicians, pharmacists and 2 technically trained raters judged necessary. ResultsReferral occurred in 74.7% of health and 46.3% of non-health responses, more often for health in every configuration (standardized difference, 28.3 percentage points; 95% CI, 18.3-37.0). Where raters judged contact unnecessary, 64.5% of health vs 27.6% of non-health responses recommended a professional (odds ratio, 17.08; 95% CI, 6.14-47.54); most of the health excess was conditional referral (46.3% vs 21.0%), and unconditional referral was 18.1% vs 6.6% (odds ratio, 4.66; 95% CI, 1.43-15.19). Where an in-person assessment was judged necessary, referral was similar (89.6% vs 84.5%). In medicines and physical health, referral was not associated with rated severity (odds ratio per point, 1.16; 95% CI, 0.53-2.55), unlike outside health (3.86; 95% CI, 1.79-8.33). The referral gap was 20.5 percentage points among configurations released in 2023 and 32.2 and 32.3 in 2025 and 2026 (4.8 percentage points per year; 95% CI, 2.3-7.2). Conclusions and RelevanceGeneral-purpose language models referred people to a professional where a visit was needed, in health as outside it, but in health also in 2 in 3 situations that physicians and pharmacists judged manageable without contact, a pattern stronger in newer models. Evaluations of these systems should include whether their advice distinguishes situations that can be deferred or managed at a distance, alongside the referral of serious cases.

papers.title: A decision-only model as a low-cost judge of medical AI answers
papers.abstract: BackgroundTesting and deploying medical AI systems at scale already results in more outputs than clinicians can review, and the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges is growing rapidly. Decision-only models, cheap and fast models that return structured probabilities rather than text, offer a potentially scalable option for that goal. MethodsIn an OSF pre-registered evaluation, we tested TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as a judge on tasks from five validated clinical benchmarks: rubric grading (HealthBench), planted clinical errors (When Rubrics Fail), risk in AI-written clinical documents (MedVAL), counseling ratings and failures (CounselBench) and physicians preferences between answers (Real-POCQi). Comparators were expert raters agreement with each other, OpenAI Decisions, GPT-6 Luna, a proposed hybrid team combining decision models and a cheap LLM and, as frontier comparators, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. The main outcome was plain agreement with the expert label. ResultsThe test comprised 25,091 units and 213,913 model calls. Jevs agreement with expert labels averaged 64.7% over six tasks. On 3,614 matched units it averaged 66.1%, against 65.0% for Opus and 60.7% for Sol, and it was non-inferior to both on four of six tasks. Jev judged the whole pool in 17 minutes for US$1.46; per judgment, it cost 1/34 of Sols price and 1/152 of Opuss. A preset cutoff held its false-alarm rate on fresh planted-error answers, and in simulation, reviewing Jevs least-sure answers first found 1.4 times the errors of a random audit. Still, omissions were hard for both: at the same false-alarm rate, Jev missed 55.6% of planted omissions and Opus 48.1%, and Opus caught 8.8 points more planted errors overall. ConclusionsAcross more than 200,000 model calls, a decision-only model was non-inferior to two frontier judges on most tasks at a small fraction of their cost and time, while reporting how sure it was of every call. With local cutoffs and expert oversight of omissions and clinical documents, judging every output of a deployed medical AI system becomes more affordable.

papers.title: Comparing Machine Learning Methods for Detecting Caregiver Burden in Transcribed Conversations with Clinicians
papers.abstract: Dementia caregivers elevated burden is associated with earlier patient institutionalization and greater caregiver morbidity, yet no standardized, objective method exists for detecting burden during routine clinical encounters. We compared four machine learning and AI approaches for detecting caregiver burden in de-identified caregiver-clinician transcripts from the COPE in PACE study using Zarit burden scores. A naive baseline predicting burden in every transcript achieved precision/F1 = 0.40/0.57. LLM prompting achieved precision/F1 = 0.43/0.60. Weak supervision achieved precision/F1 = 0.48/0.58. The fully supervised model, trained on sentence-level labels with only 1.1% burden-positive sentences, achieved precision/F1=0.19/0.25; this result is not directly comparable because of different labels and units of analysis. LLM prompting modestly outperformed weak supervision and naive baseline without fine-tuning, while class imbalance limited fully supervised sentence-level classification. Larger annotated corpora and refined labeling strategies are needed for clinical deployment.

papers.title: Algorithmic design choices as determinants of health equity: a causal simulation study of healthcare resource allocation
papers.abstract: BackgroundCare management programs increasingly rely on prediction algorithms to decide which patients receive limited healthcare resources. Because these algorithms are typically trained to predict future healthcare utilization or cost, they may systematically underidentify patients whose care-seeking behavior is suppressed by structural barriers. ObjectiveTo evaluate how three modifiable design choices (selection threshold, feature set, and training objective) affect allocation equity in care management targeting. MethodsWe constructed an analytical cohort of 201,216 adults from linked electronic health record and participant survey data in the NIH All of Us Research Program (2017-2019). Three prediction models (logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost) were trained and evaluated under simulation conditions that varied one design choice at a time while holding the others fixed. Equity was assessed using false negative rate (FNR), equal opportunity difference (EOD), and allocation rate conditional on need (an access-independent benchmark based on self-reported general health status). We also applied Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition to identify which predictors contributed most to the Black-White allocation gap. ResultsPrior utilization understated self-reported health burden among disadvantaged groups: 33% of Black and 32% of Hispanic participants reported fair or poor health, yet only 22% and 19% were classified as high utilizers. White participants showed the opposite pattern: 25% were classified as high utilizers, while only 19% reported fair or poor general health status. Under baseline design choices, all three models produced similar disparities, with uninsured participants showing the largest gap (EOD: -0.148). Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition identified prior outpatient visits as the dominant contributor to the Black-White gap in predicted allocation, with higher average emergency department utilization among Black participants partially offsetting the effect. Varying the selection threshold had little effect; disparities persisted across all thresholds. Feature set variation produced mixed and group-specific effects; removal of prior outpatient visits achieved near-zero Black-White EOD (0.001, AUC: 0.77), consistent with the Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition finding. Training objective variation produced the most substantial and consistent equity effects, with the health status objective achieving near-zero Black-White EOD (0.008, AUC: 0.69) and the survey-enriched health status condition reversing the direction of disparity for most groups. ConclusionsAlgorithmic equity in care management targeting is largely a consequence of modifiable design choices, with training objective emerging as the most impactful of the three design choices evaluated. The causal simulation framework and access-independent equity benchmark developed here provide a replicable approach for evaluating equity as a design consideration during algorithm development rather than a post-deployment correction.
